measure: US average effective tariff rate, pre-substitution (Yale Budget Lab)

points.label: Starting point
points.reason: The average tariff on imports before the 2025 changes, roughly where it had been for years.

points.label: Border, steel & “Liberation Day” tariffs
points.reason: New tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China, justified as a response to fentanyl and illegal immigration; 25% on all steel and aluminum, justified as national security; then “reciprocal” tariffs on nearly every country, justified by trade deficits.

points.label: China escalation
points.reason: Higher rates on most countries were paused for 90 days, but tariffs on Chinese goods climbed past 100% as the US and China retaliated against each other.

points.label: Truce & country deals
points.reason: A US–China truce cut the China rate, and deals with trading partners set new country-by-country rates.

points.label: Small-package exemption ends
points.reason: The duty-free allowance for small shipments ended for all countries, and new national-security tariffs were added on goods like lumber and furniture.

points.label: Food rollbacks
points.reason: Tariffs on some groceries like coffee, beef and bananas were rolled back over affordability concerns, and a new China deal lowered rates further.

points.label: New year, same level
points.reason: Rates held roughly steady heading into 2026.

points.label: Supreme Court ruling
points.reason: The Supreme Court ruled the emergency-powers law didn't authorize most of the 2025 tariffs. They were replaced the same week with a temporary 15% global tariff under a different law.

points.label: Metals tariffs restructured
points.reason: The national-security tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper were reworked.

points.label: Temporary tariff replaced
points.reason: The temporary tariff expired in July and was replaced with new 10–12.5% tariffs on about 60 trading partners, justified as a response to unfair trade practices. Unlike the temporary version, these have no built-in end date.
